difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (DFS edge classification in undirected graphs) applied in 2–3 reasoning steps (rule out cross and gray, then decide tree versus back from the colour of v), about 1.5–2 minutes; the loosely stated premise makes tree-versus-back a likely trap.
stem: Consider performing depth-first search (DFS) on an undirected and unweighted graph $G$ starting at vertex $s$. For any vertex $u$ in $G$, $d[u]$ is the length of the shortest path from $s$ to $u$. Let $(u, v)$ be an edge in $G$ such that $d[u] < d[v]$. If the edge $(u, v)$ is explored first in the direction from $u$ to $v$ during the above DFS, then $(u, v)$ becomes a \_\_\_\_\_\_ edge.

solution.quick:
In DFS of an **undirected** graph every edge is either a **tree** edge or a **back** edge, and *gray* is a vertex colour, not an edge type, so (B) and (D) are out. When $u$ scans $(u,v)$ while $v$ is still undiscovered (white), $(u,v)$ becomes a tree edge. That is the official key's answer, **(A)**.

Caveat: with $d[\cdot]$ defined as shortest-path length, $v$ can also be a gray ancestor of $u$, which makes $(u,v)$ a back edge (see the 5-vertex counterexample in Step 4). The platform keeps the official key; the premise defect is documented on this page.

steps.title: How DFS classifies an edge the first time it is scanned
steps.body:
DFS colours vertices **white** (undiscovered), **gray** (discovered, recursive call still running) and **black** (finished: every incident edge has been scanned). An undirected edge is classified the first time it is scanned, by the colour of its far endpoint.

When $u$ scans $(u,v)$, $u$ is gray and is the vertex currently being processed. There are three cases:

- $v$ is **white**: DFS discovers $v$ through this edge, so $(u,v)$ is a **tree edge**.
- $v$ is **gray**: $v$ is on the recursion stack, i.e. an ancestor of $u$ in the DFS tree, so $(u,v)$ is a **back edge**.
- $v$ is **black**: impossible here. A black $v$ has already scanned all its incident edges, including $(v,u)$, so the edge would have been explored first from $v$. That contradicts the hypothesis.

So an undirected edge that is explored first from $u$ to $v$ is either a tree edge or a back edge. This is the standard theorem that DFS on an undirected graph produces only tree and back edges.

steps.title: Eliminate (B) cross and (D) gray
steps.body:
- A **cross** edge joins two vertices neither of which is an ancestor of the other. By Step 1, the far endpoint of a first-scanned undirected edge is always white or a gray ancestor, so cross edges never occur in undirected DFS. (They do occur in DFS of directed graphs and in BFS.)
- **Gray** is one of the three vertex colours (white/gray/black) used to run DFS. It is not a type of edge.

The choice is therefore between (A) tree and (C) back.

steps.title: When the edge is a tree edge: the official answer (A)
steps.body:
$(u,v)$ becomes a tree edge exactly when $v$ is still **white** at the moment $u$ scans it. Then $u$ becomes the DFS parent of $v$.

Because $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, $|d[u] - d[v]| \le 1$. So $d[u] < d[v]$ means $d[v] = d[u] + 1$: $v$ is one step farther from $s$ than $u$. In the simplest case, the path $s - u - v$, DFS reaches $u$ first and discovers $v$ through $(u,v)$, which gives a tree edge.

The official answer key gives **(A) tree**.

For comparison, the conclusion is a theorem when the ordering $d[u] < d[v]$ refers to DFS **discovery times** (the order in which DFS first reaches vertices). Suppose $u$ is discovered before $v$ and $u$ scans $(u,v)$ first. If $v$ were already discovered at that moment, it would have been discovered while $u$ was active, so $v$ would be a descendant of $u$. DFS is now processing $u$ itself, so every descendant discovered so far has already finished (black). A black $v$ would have scanned $(v,u)$ first, which is a contradiction. So $v$ is white and $(u,v)$ is a tree edge.

steps.title: Caveat: shortest-path distances alone do not force a tree edge
steps.body:
With $d[\cdot]$ defined as in the stem (shortest-path length), a back edge is also possible, because a DFS tree need not follow shortest paths. Take vertices $s, a, u, v, w$ with the six edges $s\text{–}a$, $a\text{–}v$, $v\text{–}w$, $w\text{–}u$, $u\text{–}s$, $u\text{–}v$, and scan the adjacency lists in this order:

| Vertex | Neighbours (scan order) | $d[\cdot]$ |
|---|---|---|
| $s$ | $a, u$ | 0 |
| $a$ | $s, v$ | 1 |
| $u$ | $s, w, v$ | 1 |
| $v$ | $a, w, u$ | 2 |
| $w$ | $v, u$ | 2 |

DFS from $s$ follows the tree edges $s \to a \to v \to w \to u$. Note that $v$ goes to $w$ before it looks at $u$. At $u$:

1. $u$ scans $s$, which is gray, so $(u,s)$ is a back edge.
2. $u$ skips $w$, because that edge was already used as the tree edge $(w,u)$.
3. $u$ scans $v$. DFS at $v$ is still inside the subtree of $w$, so $v$ has not yet scanned $(v,u)$. The edge $(u,v)$ is therefore explored **first from $u$ to $v$**. Since $v$ is **gray**, $(u,v)$ becomes a **back edge**.

This happens even though $d[u] = 1 < d[v] = 2$.

A Python check confirms this. It traces this graph and runs 20 000 random small graphs with random adjacency orders. Under the shortest-path definition both tree and back edges occur; under the discovery-time reading only tree edges occur. Five vertices is the minimum for such a counterexample: $v$ must be at distance 2 (so a vertex $a$ lies between $s$ and $v$), and $u$ must hang below $v$ through a different vertex $w$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body:
Cross and gray are impossible. The official key gives **(A) tree**, which is the outcome whenever $v$ is still undiscovered when $u$ scans the edge.

Under the literal shortest-path definition of $d[\cdot]$, (C) back can also occur (Step 4), so the premise does not force a unique answer. The stem restates the textbook proof (CLRS Theorem 22.10) in which $d[u]$ is the DFS **discovery time**; with that meaning (A) is forced, so (A) is the intended answer. The platform keeps the official answer (A) and documents the premise defect.

solution.finalAnswer: **(A)** tree (official key; see the caveat in Step 4)
solution.teaching:
**DFS edge classification.** Depth-first search goes as deep as possible along each branch before it backtracks. To track its progress it colours every vertex:

- **white**: not yet discovered;
- **gray**: discovered, and its recursive call is still running (it is on the recursion stack);
- **black**: finished, meaning every incident edge has been scanned.

At any moment the gray vertices form one root-to-current path in the DFS tree. Each edge is labelled when it is first scanned, according to the colour of the vertex at the other end:

| Colour of the far end | Edge type |
|---|---|
| white | tree edge (DFS discovers that vertex through it) |
| gray | back edge (it points to an ancestor on the stack) |
| black | forward or cross edge (**directed graphs only**) |

In an **undirected** graph the black case never arises on a first scan. A black vertex has already scanned all of its edges, so the edge would have been classified from the other side. Hence undirected DFS produces **only tree and back edges**. Every non-tree edge therefore closes a cycle with the tree path, which is why DFS detects cycles in undirected graphs.

**Distances versus DFS ancestry.** In this question $d[u]$ is a BFS-style shortest-path distance. BFS trees follow shortest paths, but DFS trees generally do not: DFS may reach a vertex close to $s$ through a long detour. Being closer to $s$ therefore does not stop a vertex from having a DFS ancestor that is farther from $s$. That gap is exactly what the counterexample in Step 4 uses.

**Back to this question.** Cross and gray are ruled out immediately. The key's answer, tree, describes the case where $v$ is still white when $u$ first looks at the edge. That case is guaranteed when the ordering $d[u] < d[v]$ refers to discovery times, but shortest-path distances alone do not guarantee it.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Official key. $(u,v)$ is a tree edge whenever $v$ is still white (undiscovered) when $u$ scans it, as on the path $s - u - v$. The outcome is guaranteed if $d[u] < d[v]$ is read as DFS discovery order. Under the stem's shortest-path definition it is the typical outcome but not the only one (see Step 4).

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Cross edges never occur in DFS of an undirected graph. The far endpoint of a first-scanned edge is either white (tree) or a gray ancestor (back). Cross edges belong to directed DFS and to BFS.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Not the official answer. A back edge needs $v$ to be a gray ancestor of $u$ when $u$ scans the edge. Note that under the literal shortest-path definition of $d[\cdot]$ this can actually happen (the 5-vertex counterexample in Step 4). That is why the platform documents this premise defect next to the official answer.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: "Gray" is a vertex colour in the white/gray/black DFS bookkeeping (discovered but not finished). It is not an edge type.

solution.shortcut: Undirected DFS produces **only tree and back edges**, so cross and gray can be struck out at once. (Undirected BFS, by contrast, produces only tree and cross edges.)
solution.commonTrap: Carrying over BFS or directed-graph vocabulary. *Cross* edges occur in BFS and in directed DFS, but never in undirected DFS, and *gray* is a vertex colour. A subtler trap is assuming that a vertex farther from $s$ cannot be a DFS ancestor of a nearer one: DFS trees do not follow shortest paths.

answerVerification.independentAnswer: (A) tree under the intended reading (d[·] = DFS discovery time, as in the textbook proof the stem restates, CLRS Thm 22.10). (B) cross and (D) gray are impossible. Under the literal shortest-path wording (C) back is also attainable (5-vertex minimum); see dispute.
answerVerification.notes: Dispute resolved 2026-09-29 (official key retained, premise defect documented). History: author and blind verifier both found that the literal shortest-path definition of d[·] admits a back edge (5-vertex counterexample); the item was NEEDS_REVIEW with the official key kept. An independent adjudicator re-derived the edge rules, reproduced the counterexample, enumerated every connected graph on ≤5 vertices over all adjacency orders (18,953,037 tree vs 901,152 back outcomes; none below 5 vertices) and showed that with d[·] read as discovery time every qualifying edge is a tree edge (60,751,445/60,751,445). The stem restates the proof of CLRS Theorem 22.10, where d[u] is the discovery time, so (A) is the intended answer; the official final key keeps A and does not mark Q14 MTA (it does mark Q59 of this paper MTA). Previous verifier notes: The official key is A (tree), and the answer field keeps it. Independent verifier (blind re-solve) reached the same finding as the author: in undirected DFS an edge first scanned from u to v is a tree edge if v is white and a back edge if v is gray (an ancestor of u); a black v is impossible. The stem defines d[·] as shortest-path length from s, and DFS trees need not follow shortest paths. Verifier's independently found counterexample (it turns out to be the same 5-vertex graph as Step 4, with a different scan order at u): edges s–x, s–u, x–v, v–w, v–u, w–u with adjacency order s:[x,u], x:[s,v], v:[x,w,u], w:[v,u], u:[s,v,w]; then d[u]=1 < d[v]=2, DFS goes s→x→v→w→u, and u scans (u,v) while v is gray and has not yet scanned (v,u), so (u,v) is first explored from u to v and becomes a back edge. The Step 4 trace (edges s–a, a–v, v–w, w–u, u–s, u–v; u scans s, w, v) was also re-traced by hand and in Python and is correct. A random search over 20000 small graphs finds both tree and back outcomes under the shortest-path definition, and only tree outcomes if d[·] is DFS discovery time; an exhaustive search shows no 4-vertex counterexample exists (5 vertices is the minimum). Option C is therefore also attainable and the premise does not force A. The official key (A) was not changed. A human reviewer should confirm how this item is presented.

dispute.studentNote: GATE's official key is (A) tree. The question restates the textbook (CLRS) proof in which d[u] means DFS discovery time; with that meaning (A) is forced. dispute.intendedReading: The stem follows the proof of CLRS Theorem 22.10 (undirected DFS yields only tree and back edges), where d[u] is the DFS discovery time. Under that reading (A) tree is forced: a gray v would be an ancestor of u with an earlier discovery time.
dispute.literalPremiseFinding: With d[·] as the literal shortest-path length, (u,v) is a tree edge if v is white and a back edge if v is a gray ancestor of u. The back case occurs in 88 of the 728 connected 5-vertex graphs for some adjacency order, and never with 4 or fewer vertices.
